title: 138. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Choosing Mean Types in Applied Contexts
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Selecting the Arithmetic Mean for Equally Weighted Data
questions.learningObjective: Choose the arithmetic mean when all observations have equal importance.
questions.question: A student receives four test scores that all count equally toward the final score. Which mean should be used to find the overall score?
questions.explanation: Because the four test scores have equal weight, the overall score is found by adding the scores and dividing by \(4\). This is the arithmetic mean. The geometric mean would be appropriate for multiplicative growth factors, not for equally weighted additive scores.
questions.hint: Decide what must be preserved: a sum, a product, a weighted total, or a travel time.

questions.concept: Selecting the Weighted Mean for Unequal Contributions
questions.learningObjective: Choose the weighted mean when components contribute with different weights.
questions.question: A course grade is computed with homework worth \(20\%\), a midterm worth \(30\%\), and a final exam worth \(50\%\). Which mean is appropriate for computing the final grade?
questions.explanation: The three components do not contribute equally: homework, midterm, and final have different weights. The final grade should be computed as \(0.20H+0.30M+0.50F\), which is a weighted mean. A simple arithmetic mean would incorrectly treat all three components as equally important.
questions.hint: Check whether equal amounts, equal times, or unequal weights are involved.

questions.concept: Selecting the Geometric Mean for Growth Factors
questions.learningObjective: Choose the geometric mean when averaging multiplicative growth factors.
questions.question: An investment grows by factors \(1.2\), \(1.5\), and \(1.1\) over three equal periods. Which mean should be used to find the average growth factor per period?
questions.explanation: Growth factors combine multiplicatively. The average growth factor per period is the geometric mean \(\sqrt[3]{1.2\times 1.5\times 1.1}\). The arithmetic mean would add the factors, which does not correctly represent repeated multiplication.
questions.hint: Identify whether the situation combines additive values or multiplicative factors.

questions.concept: Selecting the Harmonic Mean for Equal-Distance Speeds
questions.learningObjective: Choose the harmonic mean when averaging speeds over equal distances.
questions.question: A car travels the first half of a journey at \(40\text{ km/h}\) and the second half at \(60\text{ km/h}\). Which mean gives the average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: The two halves are equal in distance, so the average speed is the harmonic mean \(\frac{2\times 40\times 60}{40+60}=48\text{ km/h}\). The arithmetic mean \(50\text{ km/h}\) would apply only if the car traveled for equal times at the two speeds.
questions.hint: Decide what must be preserved: a sum, a product, a weighted total, or a travel time.

questions.concept: Selecting the Weighted Mean for Combined Group Averages
questions.learningObjective: Choose the weighted mean when combining groups of different sizes.
questions.question: Class A has \(15\) students with mean score \(72\), and Class B has \(25\) students with mean score \(88\). Which mean is appropriate for the combined mean score?
questions.explanation: Use a weighted mean with group sizes as the weights, so each student contributes equally. A harmonic mean averages reciprocal rates and is not appropriate for combining group scores.
questions.hint: Check whether equal amounts, equal times, or unequal weights are involved.

questions.concept: Selecting the Geometric Mean for Multiplicative Factors
questions.learningObjective: Choose the geometric mean when averaging successive multiplicative factors.
questions.question: A quantity is multiplied by \(3\) and then by \(12\) over two equal intervals. Which mean gives the average multiplicative factor per interval?
questions.explanation: The average multiplicative factor is the geometric mean \(\sqrt{3\times 12}=\sqrt{36}=6\). The arithmetic mean \(\frac{3+12}{2}=7.5\) does not correctly represent repeated multiplication.
questions.hint: Identify whether the situation combines additive values or multiplicative factors.

questions.concept: Selecting the Arithmetic Mean for Equal-Time Speeds
questions.learningObjective: Choose the arithmetic mean when averaging speeds over equal time intervals.
questions.question: A cyclist rides for equal time intervals at \(10\text{ km/h}\) and \(20\text{ km/h}\). Which mean gives the average speed?
questions.explanation: Because the two time intervals are equal, the average speed is \(\frac{10+20}{2}=15\text{ km/h}\). This is the arithmetic mean. The harmonic mean would be used if equal distances, not equal times, were involved.
questions.hint: Decide what must be preserved: a sum, a product, a weighted total, or a travel time.

questions.concept: Selecting the Harmonic Mean for Equal-Volume Rates
questions.learningObjective: Choose the harmonic mean when averaging rates over equal amounts.
questions.question: A pump fills equal volumes at rates \(2\text{ L/min}\) and \(3\text{ L/min}\). Which mean gives the average rate over the equal volumes?
questions.explanation: The two equal volumes act like equal distances in a speed problem, so the average rate is the harmonic mean \(\frac{2\times 2\times 3}{2+3}=\frac{12}{5}=2.4\text{ L/min}\). The arithmetic mean \(2.5\text{ L/min}\) would be incorrect for equal amounts.
questions.hint: Check whether equal amounts, equal times, or unequal weights are involved.

questions.concept: Selecting the Geometric Mean for Percentage Growth
questions.learningObjective: Choose the geometric mean when averaging percentage growth over equal periods.
questions.question: A quantity grows by \(21\%\) in one period and by \(44\%\) in the next. Which mean should be used to find the average growth factor per period?
questions.explanation: The growth factors are \(1.21\) and \(1.44\). The average growth factor is the geometric mean \(\sqrt{1.21\times 1.44}=\sqrt{1.7424}=1.32\), corresponding to an average growth of \(32\%\) per period. The arithmetic mean would incorrectly average the percentages directly.
questions.hint: Identify whether the situation combines additive values or multiplicative factors.

questions.concept: Selecting the Arithmetic Mean for Equally Reliable Measurements
questions.learningObjective: Choose the arithmetic mean when repeated measurements have equal reliability.
questions.question: A set of repeated measurements of the same quantity are equally reliable. Which mean is most appropriate for the best estimate?
questions.explanation: When repeated measurements have equal reliability, each measurement contributes equally to the best estimate. The best estimate is therefore the arithmetic mean, found by adding the measurements and dividing by their number. Harmonic and geometric means apply to different contexts, such as equal-distance rates or multiplicative growth.
questions.hint: Check whether any measurement has been assigned a greater influence than another.
